name: Capsule
description: The outermost protective layer of the E. coli bacterium. It provides structural support, prevents dehydration, and protects the cell from phagocytosis.

name: Cell Wall
description: A rigid layer of peptidoglycan located just inside the capsule. It gives the bacterium its shape and protects against osmotic pressure.

name: Plasma Membrane
description: A phospholipid bilayer just inside the cell wall. It controls the transport of substances in and out of the cell and houses enzymes for energy generation.

name: Cytoplasm
description: The gel-like substance enclosed within the cell membrane. It contains the nucleoid, ribosomes, and various metabolic enzymes.

name: Nucleoid (DNA)
description: The irregularly shaped region within the cell where the genetic material (circular DNA) is localized.

name: Ribosomes
description: Complex molecular machines found within the cytoplasm that serve as the site of biological protein synthesis (translation).

name: Flagella
description: Long, whip-like appendages used for cellular locomotion. They act like propellers to move the bacterium through liquid.

name: Pili / Fimbriae
description: Hair-like appendages on the surface of the cell used for attachment to surfaces and other cells, aiding in infection and DNA transfer.

name: GamGFP (DSB Sensor)
description: A fusion of bacteriophage Mu Gam and Green Fluorescent Protein (GFP) developed in the 2013 eLife paper. Gam is a DNA end-binding protein. When fused to GFP, it forms bright green foci exactly at the sites of double-strand breaks.

reference.title: Shee, C., Cox, B. D., Gu, F., Luengas, E. M., Joshi, M. C., Chiu, L. Y., Magnan, D., Rosenberg, S. M., Frisch, R. L., & Hastings, P. J. (2013). Engineered proteins detect spontaneous DNA breakage in human and bacterial cells. eLife, 2, e01222.

name: TetR-mCherry Reporter
description: A fusion of the Tet Repressor and mCherry (red fluorescent protein). It binds to a specific chromosomal array (tetO) to mark a fixed genomic locus, forming a red fluorescent focus.

reference.title: Shee, C., Cox, B. D., Gu, F., Luengas, E. M., Joshi, M. C., Chiu, L. Y., Magnan, D., Rosenberg, S. M., Frisch, R. L., & Hastings, P. J. (2013). Engineered proteins detect spontaneous DNA breakage in human and bacterial cells. eLife, 2, e01222.

name: Co-localization (Yellow)
description: When a double-strand break occurs exactly at the marked tetO locus, GamGFP (green) and TetR-mCherry (red) bind to the exact same region. The overlapping fluorescent signals create a yellow focus, visually proving GamGFP specifically targets DSBs.

reference.title: Shee, C., Cox, B. D., Gu, F., Luengas, E. M., Joshi, M. C., Chiu, L. Y., Magnan, D., Rosenberg, S. M., Frisch, R. L., & Hastings, P. J. (2013). Engineered proteins detect spontaneous DNA breakage in human and bacterial cells. eLife, 2, e01222.

name: Plasmid DNA
description: Small, extra-chromosomal circular DNA molecules. The red plasmid represents a reporter plasmid expressing TetR-mCherry, and the larger one can represent an F conjugative plasmid used to study replication fork collapses.

reference.title: Shee, C., Cox, B. D., Gu, F., Luengas, E. M., Joshi, M. C., Chiu, L. Y., Magnan, D., Rosenberg, S. M., Frisch, R. L., & Hastings, P. J. (2013). Engineered proteins detect spontaneous DNA breakage in human and bacterial cells. eLife, 2, e01222.

name: Double-Strand Break (DSB)
description: A severe form of DNA damage where both strands of the double helix are severed. If left unrepaired, it can lead to cell death or genomic instability.

reference.title: Shee, C., Cox, B. D., Gu, F., Luengas, E. M., Joshi, M. C., Chiu, L. Y., Magnan, D., Rosenberg, S. M., Frisch, R. L., & Hastings, P. J. (2013). Engineered proteins detect spontaneous DNA breakage in human and bacterial cells. eLife, 2, e01222.

name: I-SceI Endonuclease
description: A restriction enzyme used in the eLife paper experiments. It induces a targeted, site-specific double-strand break near the tetO array, allowing the researchers to control exactly where and when the DNA breaks.

reference.title: Shee, C., Cox, B. D., Gu, F., Luengas, E. M., Joshi, M. C., Chiu, L. Y., Magnan, D., Rosenberg, S. M., Frisch, R. L., & Hastings, P. J. (2013). Engineered proteins detect spontaneous DNA breakage in human and bacterial cells. eLife, 2, e01222.

name: RecBCD Enzyme
description: A bacterial exonuclease that normally degrades broken DNA ends. GamGFP competes directly with RecBCD by capping the DNA ends, preventing degradation and allowing the break to be visualized.

reference.title: Engineered proteins detect spontaneous DNA breakage in human and bacterial cells (eLife 2013)
